lead: A discrete-time Markov chain is a random process that moves between states at integer times. Its defining feature is the Markov property: once the present state is known, the past tells you nothing more about the next state. One matrix, the transition matrix P, stores every one-step probability. Powers of P give two-step, three-step and n-step probabilities. Weather forecasts, queue lengths at a ticket counter, credit ratings and page-rank all use this model because it turns a random story into matrix arithmetic.
prereq: You need: conditional probability from Unit 2, joint distributions from Unit 4, and 7.1 on random processes.

blocks.text: Take a system observed at integer times n = 0, 1, 2, …. At each time it sits in one state. The random variable Xₙ is the state at time n. The set of possible states is the state space S; write S = {1, 2, …, N} when it has N states. A discrete-time Markov chain has the Markov property: for every i and j, P(X<sub>n+1</sub> = j | X<sub>n</sub> = i, past) = P(X<sub>n+1</sub> = j | X<sub>n</sub> = i). The left side conditions on the whole past; the right side uses only the present. The chain forgets the past once the present is fixed.

The chain is homogeneous if P(X<sub>n+1</sub> = j | X<sub>n</sub> = i) does not depend on n. Then define P<sub>ij</sub> = P(X<sub>n+1</sub> = j | X<sub>n</sub> = i). The matrix P has rows labelled by current state i and columns by next state j. Its entry in row i, column j is P<sub>ij</sub>. Every entry satisfies P<sub>ij</sub> ≥ 0, and every row sums to 1: Σ<sub>j</sub> P<sub>ij</sub> = 1. The row sum is 1 because from state i the next state must be one of the states j. Some syllabi call P the transition probability matrix. The weather chain in the figure uses states S (sunny) and R (rainy).

The n-step transition probability is P<sub>ij</sub><sup>(n)</sup> = P(X<sub>n</sub> = j | X<sub>0</sub> = i). For n = 2, condition on the middle state X<sub>1</sub> = k and sum over k. This gives the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation P<sub>ij</sub><sup>(n+m)</sup> = Σ<sub>k</sub> P<sub>ik</sub><sup>(n)</sup> P<sub>kj</sub><sup>(m)</sup>. The sum runs over every state k; it is the probability of going from i to k in n steps and then k to j in m steps.

In matrix form, P(n) = Pn, the ordinary n-fold matrix product. So P² = P × P, not the elementwise square. The (i, j) entry of P² is Σk Pik Pkj. Three-step probabilities come from P³ = P² × P. Every Pn is again a transition matrix: its entries are non-negative and its rows sum to 1. This is the engine of the chapter: one P generates every future probability. Steady-state limits are in 7.5.

State j is accessible from state i if P<sub>ij</sub><sup>(n)</sup> > 0 for some n ≥ 0. States i and j communicate if i is accessible from j and j is accessible from i. Communication splits the state space into classes. A chain is irreducible if it has one class: every state can reach every other state.

A state i is recurrent if the probability of returning to i at some future time, starting from i, is 1. It is transient if that probability is less than 1. A recurrent state is positive recurrent if its expected return time is finite. In a finite irreducible chain every state is positive recurrent.

The period of state i is d(i) = gcd{ n ≥ 1 : P<sub>ii</sub><sup>(n)</sup> > 0 }, the greatest common divisor of the times at which a return is possible. If d(i) = 1 the state is aperiodic. A self-loop P<sub>ii</sub> > 0 makes d(i) = 1. A state with P<sub>ii</sub> = 1 is absorbing: once entered, the chain never leaves. An irreducible positive recurrent aperiodic chain is called ergodic in some syllabi.

Keep the words apart. Accessible is one-way; communicate is two-way. Recurrent is about return probability; positive recurrent is about finite mean return time. Periodic is about the gcd of return times, not about whether a return is possible.

figure.caption: The weather chain: each arrow is a one-step probability from its tail state, and the two rows of P sum to 1.

spec.aria: A directed graph with two nodes S and R; self-loops and cross edges are labelled 0.8, 0.2, 0.7 and 0.3.

examples.question: A weather chain has states S (sunny) and R (rainy). Its one-step transition matrix is P = [[0.8, 0.2], [0.3, 0.7]], with rows S, R. (a) Draw the state diagram. (b) Find P². (c) Classify the chain: irreducible? aperiodic? recurrent? positive recurrent?
steps: Read the rows. From S: P<sub>SS</sub> = 0.8 and P<sub>SR</sub> = 0.2. From R: P<sub>RS</sub> = 0.3 and P<sub>RR</sub> = 0.7. Each row sums to 1.0. Draw self-loops S→S and R→R, and cross arrows S→R with 0.2 and R→S with 0.3.
Compute the (S, S) entry of P²: P<sub>SS</sub>P<sub>SS</sub> + P<sub>SR</sub>P<sub>RS</sub> = 0.8×0.8 + 0.2×0.3 = 0.64 + 0.06 = 0.70.
Compute the (S, R) entry: P<sub>SS</sub>P<sub>SR</sub> + P<sub>SR</sub>P<sub>RR</sub> = 0.8×0.2 + 0.2×0.7 = 0.16 + 0.14 = 0.30. Row S sums to 1.00.
Compute the (R, S) entry: P<sub>RS</sub>P<sub>SS</sub> + P<sub>RR</sub>P<sub>RS</sub> = 0.3×0.8 + 0.7×0.3 = 0.24 + 0.21 = 0.45.
Compute the (R, R) entry: P<sub>RS</sub>P<sub>SR</sub> + P<sub>RR</sub>P<sub>RR</sub> = 0.3×0.2 + 0.7×0.7 = 0.06 + 0.49 = 0.55. Row R sums to 1.00. So P² = [[0.70, 0.30], [0.45, 0.55]].
Irreducible: S reaches R in one step with probability 0.2, and R reaches S in one step with probability 0.3. All states communicate, so there is one class.
Aperiodic: P<sub>SS</sub> = 0.8 > 0, so S has a self-loop and period 1. P<sub>RR</sub> = 0.7 > 0, so R also has period 1.
Recurrent and positive recurrent: the chain is finite and irreducible, so every state is recurrent. A finite irreducible chain is positive recurrent.
examples.answer: P² = [[0.70, 0.30], [0.45, 0.55]]; the chain is irreducible, aperiodic and positive recurrent.

traps: Rows sum to 1, not columns. This book uses row-stochastic P. A column-stochastic version is the transpose; check which convention your exam uses.
P² is the matrix product P × P, not the elementwise square. Elementwise squaring gives wrong two-step probabilities.
P<sub>ij</sub> = 0 does not mean j is unreachable. Reachability allows some n ≥ 1 through other states.
Period is the gcd of return times. A state can have P<sub>ii</sub> = 0 and still be aperiodic if returns occur at times with gcd 1, such as 2 and 3.
Irreducible does not mean recurrent for infinite state spaces. A finite irreducible chain is recurrent and positive recurrent; an infinite irreducible chain can be transient.

quiz.q: State the Markov property in words and in symbols.
quiz.a: Given the present state, the past adds no information about the next state: P(X<sub>n+1</sub> = j | X<sub>n</sub> = i, past) = P(X<sub>n+1</sub> = j | X<sub>n</sub> = i).

quiz.q: Why must every row of a homogeneous one-step transition matrix sum to 1?
quiz.a: From current state i, the next state must be exactly one of the possible states j. The probabilities P<sub>ij</sub> over all j form a probability distribution, so Σ<sub>j</sub> P<sub>ij</sub> = 1.

quiz.q: A chain on states 1, 2, 3 has P = [[0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1], [1, 0, 0]]. Is it irreducible? Find the period of each state.
quiz.a: It is irreducible: the arrows form the cycle 1→2→3→1, so every state reaches every other. A return to any state is possible only at times 3, 6, 9, …, so the gcd is 3. Every state has period 3.

quiz.q: For P = [[0.5, 0.5], [0, 1]], classify the two states and say whether the chain is irreducible.
quiz.a: State 2 has P<sub>22</sub> = 1, so it is absorbing and recurrent. State 1 has probability 0.5 of moving to 2 and never returning, so state 1 is transient. The chain is not irreducible because state 2 cannot reach state 1.

quiz.q: Give the difference between a recurrent state and a transient state.
quiz.a: A recurrent state has return probability 1: starting there, the chain returns eventually with certainty. A transient state has return probability less than 1: there is positive probability of never returning.

quiz.q: A finite irreducible chain has P<sub>ii</sub> > 0 for every state i. What can you say about its periodicity and recurrence?
quiz.a: Each self-loop gives period 1, so the chain is aperiodic. Finite irreducible gives recurrence and positive recurrence. Hence the chain is ergodic under the definition used in some syllabi.

beyond: Not for the exam. Markov chains drive page-rank, speech recognition, weather models and credit-risk migration. Search 'Markov chain Monte Carlo', 'hidden Markov model Viterbi' and 'Markov decision process'. The same transition matrix idea becomes a generator matrix in continuous time in 7.6.
